transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. I guess what brings me in is… I feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. Like I’ll finish one thing at school, or at home, and before I even think about it I’m already jumping into the next thing. I can’t seem to shut myself off.

And, you know, being a special ed teacher, there’s always something happening anyway—forms, kids needing help, someone popping into the room—so sometimes I tell myself it’s just the job. But even when I get home, it’s like I keep going. One task to the next, no real stopping point. It’s exhausting, honestly.
Have you been needing less sleep than usual and still feeling rested?

Um… needing less sleep and feeling rested? I don’t know that I’d put it that way. I mean, sleep is kind of… it varies, and honestly with school stuff I can get caught up thinking about the next day, but “less sleep and still rested” doesn’t really sound like something I’ve noticed.

I’m usually not walking around thinking, “Wow, I’m fine on no sleep,” if that’s what you mean. Although sometimes the kids at school have more energy than I do, which is saying something. But no, I’m not sure I’ve had that.
Have there been times when you felt unusually up or euphoric?

Unusually up or euphoric… I’m not sure. I mean, I have good days, sure—like if a kid finally gets something we’ve been working on for weeks, that can put me in a great mood. Last year I had this student who—well, anyway, those moments stick with you.

But if you mean like out-of-the-blue, over-the-top happy or almost high, I don’t really know that I’ve noticed that. It’s more just… regular good moods when something good happens, I guess.
Do you often have trouble sustaining attention on tasks, like paperwork, lesson planning, or conversations?

Hmm… trouble sustaining attention? I’m not totally sure how to answer that. Paperwork is definitely not my favorite thing, but whose is, right? Especially in special ed, there’s always a stack of forms that seems to grow when you’re not looking.

Lesson planning, I mean, sometimes I can sit with it, sometimes I end up thinking about three other classroom things I need to fix—like seating, or whether a certain kid needs a different visual schedule, or if I forgot to email someone. And conversations… I try to pay attention, I really do. My wife says—well, no, maybe that’s a different thing.

So… I guess I notice it here and there, but I don’t know if I’d say it’s the main problem or anything. It’s hard to separate from just having a busy job.
Did these symptoms start after a particular stressful event or major change in your life?

No, I don’t think it started after one particular stressful thing or change. I mean, life changes can make things feel louder, sure, and family stuff can throw anybody off—but this goes way back.

My mother used to joke that when I was in elementary school I was practically teaching the class from my seat, because I was always out of my chair or talking, or jumping in before the teacher even finished giving directions. She’d tell that story at family dinners, usually when I was already interrupting someone, which… okay, fair.

So no, this wasn’t something that suddenly showed up in adulthood or after a family change. It was kind of already me, for as long as I can remember.
Do you notice these same problems outside of work too, like at home or in social situations?

Yeah… it’s not just work. I mean, work is where it’s gotten really official, I guess—like serious enough that I got put on a corrective plan, which was embarrassing. And frustrating, because I’m not trying to make things harder for anyone. I’m usually trying to help, and then somehow I end up making people feel like they can’t count on me.

At home it shows up too. My wife says the caregiving routines are harder because everyone’s already juggling so much, and then they have to manage my energy on top of it. Which… that’s hard to hear. I don’t mean to be one more thing people have to manage.

And socially, I don’t know, I can tell sometimes people get worn out. I start feeling like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and my family, even when my intentions are good. That part really bothers me.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

Worrying… I’m not sure. I mean, everybody worries, right? Especially when you’ve got work stuff and home stuff and all the little things that pile up—like bills, schedules, whether I remembered to send in some form… although that’s more “did I do the thing” than sitting there worrying, I guess.

I don’t know if I spend a lot of time worrying when there isn’t a problem. I’d have to think about that. Sometimes my mind is busy, but I’m not sure I’d call it worry exactly.
Do you often interrupt people before they’ve finished speaking?

Yes. Yeah, I do. More than I’d like to admit.

It happens with colleagues, with parents at work, and definitely at home with my wife and our relative. I’ll hear part of what someone’s saying and my brain goes, “Oh, I know where this is going, I can help,” and then I jump in before they’re done. Sometimes I’m trying to clarify or solve it, but it comes out like I’m talking over them or taking charge.

And then later I realize they hadn’t even finished their thought. It’s not that I don’t care what they’re saying—I actually do—but I get ahead of them, if that makes sense.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive type. The patient describes longstanding hyperactive/impulsive symptoms since elementary school, including being constantly 'on the go,' difficulty stopping from one task to the next, interrupting others, blurting/jumping in before directions were finished, and being out of his seat/talking excessively in childhood. Symptoms occur across settings (work, home, social situations) and are causing clinically significant impairment, including a corrective plan at work and strain in family and colleague relationships. Bipolar and anxiety-spectrum explanations were not supported: he denied decreased need for sleep, euphoria, sudden episodic onset, and did not endorse pervasive worry as the main issue.
